\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Test-time compute scaling complements model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling}: repeated sampling with majority voting \cite{wang2023selfconsistency}, best-of-$N$ with learned verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, brown2024monkeys}, and extended chain-of-thought \cite{muennighoff2025s1} produce large gains on reasoning and code generation.
These successes share a structural prerequisite: the output space admits either exact equivalence classes (multiple-choice, numeric answers) or execution-based verification (code).
Named entity recognition (NER) breaks both assumptions.
The output is a set of typed entities; two samples from the same input routinely extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and no external oracle can adjudicate correctness at test time.
Without equivalence classes, majority voting reduces to heuristic frequency counting; without a verifier, best-of-$N$ requires a reliable proxy signal.
This structural mismatch raises a concrete question: can self-consistency signals that estimate quality well for reasoning tasks also \textit{select} better outputs or \textit{construct} better entity sets for structured generation?
We investigate this question for NER and validate the core findings on SQL parsing, treating NER as a representative instance of the broader set-valued generation problem.

The question has practical stakes beyond information extraction.
Hallucination detection methods such as SelfCheckGPT \cite{manakul2023selfcheckgpt} and FActScore \cite{min2023factscore} rely on cross-sample consistency to verify individual claims: if a model's outputs agree, the shared content is presumed factual.
This reasoning assumes entity-level self-verification works, that a model can reliably distinguish correct extractions from incorrect ones through self-judgment or re-prompting.
We show this assumption fails.
Three independent probes (entity self-judgment, multi-round re-prompting, latent-space aggregation) all yield chance-level or negative results for a fine-tuned 8B model on NER.
Recent work \cite{yao2026consistency} demonstrates that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy across benchmarks but does not diagnose \textit{when} or \textit{why} this correlation breaks down at the selection level.
Our diagnostic framework fills this gap: four failure modes (degeneracy, low agreement, false agreement, LP compression) explain why strong instance-level correlation coexists with negligible sample-level selection gain.

We call this disparity the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
Five quality estimation (QE) signals achieve rank correlations up to $\rho{=}0.45$ and AUROC up to 0.82 with oracle F1, yet no signal outperforms greedy decoding on SciERC ($p{>}0.05$ for all comparisons).
Only log-probability (LP) achieves a positive selection gain, and only on Few-NERD ($+1.39$\,pp; Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.019$, selection family $k{=}19$).
To test whether entity-level methods can close this gap, we evaluated seven approaches: entity self-judgment (ESJ), multi-round self-consistency (MRSC), latent-space aggregation (LSC), heterogeneous temperature sampling (Het-T), adaptive sampling budget (ASB), self-consistency distillation (SCD), and a supervised entity verifier.
No method produces statistically significant F1 improvement over majority vote on any tested configuration (Appendix~\ref{app:method_coverage}).
Collectively, these experiments span three NER datasets and two model families, though individual methods were tested on subsets of this matrix.
ESJ achieves AUROC of 0.51 (indistinguishable from chance), while frequency-based agreement reaches 0.87.
MRSC produces $P(\text{yes})$ separation of 0.0006 between correct and incorrect entities.
The supervised verifier achieves entity-level AUC of 0.923 but translates to only $+0.30$\,pp F1, with negative cross-dataset transfer.
A supervised hidden-state probe achieves entity-level AUROC${=}0.63$\textendash$0.88$ across three datasets from a single forward pass, exceeding prompt-based self-judgment (${=}0.51$) but not uniformly exceeding multi-sample agreement (${=}0.87$)---an introspection boundary modulated by task complexity (\S\ref{sec:mechanistic}).

These findings rest on controlled experiments across four NER benchmarks (SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}), two model families (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B), a Qwen3-4B ablation, and sample sizes $N {\in} \{2, \ldots, 32\}$.
We extend to Qwen2.5-72B in the zero-shot regime to test whether the capability ceiling persists at larger scale.
Relation extraction (RE) on SciERC reveals a task-complexity boundary: compound error propagation (${\approx}44$\% zero-F1) weakens all signals, though conditional filtering restores structural signal advantage (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Cross-task validation on Spider SQL parsing (GPT-5.5, $n{=}196$) confirms the diagnostic cascade: degeneracy reaches 87.2\%, and the F1 failure mode dominates.
Our prescriptive analysis identifies three escape routes that work precisely because they bypass entity-level self-verification: LP-weighted entity construction ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD, Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.006$; $+1.02$\,pp on SciERC, $p{=}0.004$, directionally consistent but $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.20$), cross-model ensemble ($+0.42$\,pp), and LP-based selection restricted to low-degeneracy regimes.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{Overview of the correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals estimate instance quality ($\rho$ up to 0.45; Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}). \textbf{Center}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates, so selection cannot outperform greedy. \textbf{Right}: LP-weighted entity construction ($\theta{=}2/N$) bypasses the bottleneck ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Diagnostic framework.}
    A four-stage cascade (QE $\to$ degeneracy $\to$ agreement fidelity $\to$ LP compression) explaining where and why self-consistency fails for structured generation (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}, \S\ref{sec:discussion}).

    \item \textbf{Self-verification ceiling evidence.}
    Seven entity-level methods, tested across three NER datasets and two model families, all fail to close the correlation-selection gap, constituting systematic evidence for a capability ceiling in entity-level self-verification (\S\ref{sec:mechanistic}, \S\ref{sec:adaptive}).

    \item \textbf{Introspection gap.}
    A supervised probe achieves entity-level AUROC${=}0.63$\textendash$0.88$ (GroupKFold CV), exceeding self-judgment (${=}0.51$) but falling below multi-sample agreement (${=}0.87$) on two of three datasets---hidden states encode partial entity quality inaccessible through prompting (\S\ref{sec:mechanistic}).

    \item \textbf{Prescriptive escape routes.}
    Entity-level construction ($+1.02$\,--\,$1.40$\,pp), cross-model ensemble ($+0.42$\,pp), and regime-specific LP selection ($+1.39$\,pp) bypass entity-level self-verification; a degeneracy threshold $\theta_{\text{crit}}{=}0.70$ predicts when gains vanish (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}, \S\ref{sec:theory}).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{abstract}
Test-time compute scaling through repeated sampling yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning and code generation, yet for structured information extraction (IE), where outputs are entity sets with partial overlap, a persistent gap separates quality estimation from sample selection.
We ask whether entity-level agreement signals can bridge this gap.
Across seven methods spanning self-judgment, self-refinement, latent consistency, heterogeneous verification, adaptive budgeting, distillation, and supervised classification, we find that no entity-level agreement signal reliably improves selection for named entity recognition (NER), relation extraction (RE), or Text-to-SQL.
Quality estimation signals correlate with oracle F1 ($\rho$ up to 0.45, AUROC up to 0.82) yet no signal selects better than greedy decoding.
The failure is systematic: a four-stage diagnostic cascade (quality estimation $\to$ degeneracy $\to$ agreement fidelity $\to$ log-probability compression) localizes where and why selection breaks down, with cross-task validation on SQL parsing (87.2\% output degeneracy).
A hidden-state linear probe achieves entity-level discrimination (area under the ROC curve [AUROC] $0.63$\textendash$0.88$, dataset-dependent) from a single forward pass, consistently exceeding prompt-based self-evaluation (AUROC 0.51) but matching multi-sample agreement ($0.87$) only on the simplest task.
These negative results delineate where self-consistency (SC) does succeed for IE: through paths that bypass entity-level agreement.
Log-probability selection improves F1 by $+1.39$\,pp on Few-NERD (Holm-adjusted $p{=}0.019$, selection family $k{=}19$), entity-level construction via weighted voting gains $+1.02$\textendash$1.40$\,pp, and cross-model ensembles add $+0.42$\,pp on Few-NERD.
Each exploits sequence-level or cross-model signals rather than entity-level self-verification.
A degeneracy decomposition confirms SC gain vanishes once output degeneracy exceeds 70\%.
\end{abstract}

\section{Why Self-Verification Fails}\label{sec:mechanistic}

The diagnostic cascade (\S\ref{sec:method}) identifies \textit{where} self-consistency fails; this section probes \textit{why} by testing whether models can self-verify at the entity level.
We evaluate self-verification and diagnostic probes on Qwen2.5-7B fine-tuned for NER ($N{=}8$, seed 42; full results in Appendix~\ref{app:self_verification}).

\paragraph{Entity Self-Judgment (ESJ).}
For each extracted entity, we prompt the generating model: ``Is [\textit{entity}] a [\textit{type}] entity in this sentence?''
Entity-level AUROC is $0.512$---indistinguishable from chance---with P(yes$|$correct)${=}0.500$ and P(yes$|$incorrect)${=}0.500$.
ESJ-weighted construction degrades F1 to $0.711$ (vs.\ greedy $0.794$).

\paragraph{Multi-Round Self-Consistency (MRSC).}
Re-prompting on disputed entities (agreement ${<}0.6$) with focused verification yields P(yes) separation of $0.0006$ between gold and non-gold entities ($0.5003$ vs.\ $0.4997$).
MRSC best F1 ($0.763$) falls below greedy.

\paragraph{Latent Self-Consistency (LSC).}
Mean-pooled final-layer hidden states ($d{=}3584$) provide per-sample latent representations.
Centroid selection ($0.759$) underperforms greedy ($0.794$); latent entity confidence ($0.839$) outperforms majority vote ($0.792$) but does not close the oracle gap ($0.882$).

\paragraph{Hidden-state probe.}
A logistic regression on mean-pooled final-layer hidden states at entity spans achieves AUROC $0.636$ (Few-NERD), $0.882$ (CoNLL), $0.630$ (SciERC), evaluated with GroupKFold CV (5-fold ${\times}$ 3 seeds, groups${=}$source instance to prevent entity-level leakage; Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}).
All three exceed ESJ ($0.51$); only CoNLL approaches frequency agreement ($0.868$).
Cross-dataset transfer is weak: leave-one-dataset-out AUROC drops to $0.559$ (Few-NERD${\to}$CoNLL) and $0.671$ (CoNLL${\to}$Few-NERD), indicating dataset-specific rather than universal encoding.
At the sample level, an MLP probe closes only 13.9\% of the oracle gap on SciERC (Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}).
